implementation_notes: Mockito creates the double from an interface or a non-final class with mock()/@Mock and covers both directions of the pattern: when(...).thenReturn(...)/thenThrow(...) programmes behaviour, verify(mock).method(args) and InOrder verify the interactions, and ArgumentCaptor captures arguments for further assertions. Mockito 3.x requires Java 8 and reads as action-then-verification rather than record/replay; a hand-written double is only needed for final classes or final/static members when the inline mock maker is unavailable.
pitfalls: Unstubbed calls on a Mockito mock return null/0/false, so a missing verify() or a forgotten stub can pass silently; use strict stubs or the strictness settings to surface unused and missing interactions.
final classes and methods and static members are not mockable with the subclass mock maker - the inline mock maker or a wrapper you own is required.
Argument matchers must cover all arguments of a call once one is used; mixing raw values with any()/eq() throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException rather than failing the assertion.

variants.name: EasyMock record/replay control
variants.implementation_notes: EasyMock is the original dynamic mock object generator and keeps the record/replay protocol: createMock() returns the double, calls recorded on it in record mode become the expected interactions (with andReturn/andThrow/once/times), replay(mock) switches it into checking, and verify(mock) performs the final check. Choose it for the stricter model - every unexpected call fails immediately - or in codebases that predate Mockito, which was originally built on top of EasyMock's code.
pitfalls: The record/replay split is a learnability trap: calling the mock before replay() silently records an expectation instead of failing, and forgetting verify() skips the final check.
EasyMock rejects unexpected calls immediately, which is stricter than Mockito but also couples the test to the exact sequence; relax deliberately with niceMock() or checkOrder(false).
